item.content:encoded:
Sox slugger Mickey Gasper's motivation stems from his roots in Merrimack
Merrimack's Mickey Gasper has become a fan favorite at Fenway Park, with his baseball journey taking him from high school to the Nashua Silver Knights through the minor leagues and finally to the Boston Red Sox.
Gasper grew up in Merrimack, about an hour away from Fenway.
"For me, playing with a little chip on my shoulder helps me," he told News 9.
Gasper's story is familiar to Granite Staters now, but many still ask how he can go from playing T-ball to consistently hitting homers for the Red Sox.
"A lot of work," he said.
>> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go <<
That work ethic was taught by his parents, Livia and Mick, who moved from New Jersey to Merrimack in 2001 when Mickey was about 5 years old.
"He is tenacious, and the resilience started growing at a young age," Livia Gasper said.
"He was competitive in T-ball," his father said. "One day, he made a great play. The coach of the other team said, 'We don't play outs.' And Mickey is like (making an appalled expression)."
"If there's anything that somebody from the Northeast does, it's that you do play with a chip on your shoulder," Mickey Gasper said. "A lot of people have doubted my process just in the last two years."
"He had bunk beds in his room, and I found it taped up on the flat, and it says, 'I'm not good enough,'" his father said.
Mickey Gasper worked to become good enough to play for the Merrimack High School Tomahawks.
"A lot of elite high school players rely on talent. He never did," said Nick Jaskolka, his high school coach. "That's a rare makeup for a high-end player."
That makeup has been put to the test. Mickey Gasper is currently having a breakout season at 30 years old in his second stint with the Red Sox.
Two years ago, he made his major league debut with Boston after more than five years in the minors. His family was in the stands for the first few games, making the trip from New Jersey, where they moved from New Hampshire in 2019.
But Gasper went 0-for-18 and was sent back down to the minors.
"We actually have not been back to Boston," his mother said.
"I'm staying away from Boston," his father said. "I feel like I was the kiss of death."
What has happened in Boston this summer is nothing short of remarkable. Recalled from AAA on Aug. 17, Mickey Gasper hit his first home run in a Red Sox uniform two years after his debut.
It was the first of three straight games with a homer -- six in 12 games -- for one of the best months in the history of baseball. His stats were up there with the likes of Ted Williams and Barry Bonds.
"It's cool," Mickey Gasper said. "It's something you can't live on. It's a month's stretch."
On the bottom of the bat he used to get all those hits is a picture of him and his father.
"It's very humbling," his father said. "It's been a lifelong love for baseball."
Despite that amazing run, he was sent back down on Saturday, Aug. 29. He didn't have to report to Worcester until the following Tuesday, so he visited his parents.
"First thing I said was, I'm going to go back to Freehold for the day just to be able to spend time with them," he said.
"We definitely felt the heaviness," his mother said. "We were actually supposed to go to the game on Sunday. I made a big old vat of sauce and meatballs."
"Short pasta. Against my request," Mickey Gasper said. "I like spaghetti. I'm a spaghetti guy."
This AAA stint was shorter than the pasta his mom made. During that dinner, Mickey Gasper's phone was ringing. It was the Red Sox on the other end, saying he was going back up. In his first at-bat, he hit another home run.
"He makes good meatballs," his father said.
"We go together from what feels like the lowest of lows to the highest of highs, and on that day, it was in a span of 12 hours," his mother said. "We were in tears."
"I thank my family for everything. Just being around them is…," Mickey Gasper said before trailing off.
Mickey Gasper's efforts helped the Red Sox clinch a playoff spot. Like him, the team turned things around this year. The Sox were 14 games below .500 in late June, and if the season ended today, they would play a best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where his parents have been this year.
Mick and Livia Gasper could bring the pasta and meatballs to him next time.

item.content:encoded:
On the edge of the wind-scoured Salt Lake Valley, between rows of gray and white houses and sunbaked driveways, you can find a little taste of Fenway Park.
A housing subdivision in Herriman, Utah, is turning heads online for its streets, each of which bears the name of a Red Sox star from the annals of team history: Pesky Lane, Pedroia Street, and Varitek Drive, to name a few.
The names, which could be ripped straight from the banners on Van Ness Street, stand out in a place like Herriman, a Salt Lake City suburb 500 miles from the nearest Major League Baseball stadium. There’s little else to suggest Copper Fields, a neat grid of roughly 200 houses completed by Edge Homes in 2024, has a link to Boston.
But once social media caught wind of the Sox-heavy ‘hood over the weekend, fans were ablaze with speculation.
“Ready to blow my savings and move to Utah so I can live on Pedroia Street,” one commenter wrote on X, posting an image of a three-bed, three-bath home on sale for $669,000 (slightly cheaper than a 700-square-foot condo in the South End).
“[I don’t care] about getting priced out of Boston,” opined Anna Caruso of Section 10, a Red Sox podcast, beneath a photo of the development. “You’ll find me here.”
Another commenter said that, in person, the neighborhood is “brand-new and pretty nice,” though “all of the houses look basically the same.”
“I wonder what [percentage] of families that live here have no idea what the streets mean,” they added.
So, who’s behind all these names? There’s not much of a Red Sox connection in the area to speak of, aside from the fact that a young David Ortiz played with Salt Lake’s minor league team while still a Minnesota Twins prospect.
But that didn’t matter to Brandon Parr, the Edge Homes project manager who selected the names. Parr, 47, was born and raised in Utah — but he lives and breathes the Red Sox all the same.
“I liked Wade Boggs a lot, and he just happened to play for them, so I became a fan,” he said. “The rest is history.”
When Parr got the chance to name an entire new subdivision, his vision was clear.
“I don’t think anybody on my team really knew what I was doing until they saw the first flat be recorded [on the master plan],” he said.
Parr made sure to include a (Wade) Boggs Way, as well as a (Jerry) Remy Road, named after the late broadcaster and former player, and a Xander (Bogaerts) Lane. The neighborhood even has a Yawkey Way, named after the controversial Red Sox owner whose name once marked what is now Jersey Street. (Edge Homes seems to have missed the memo on that one.)
Plenty of fans online wondered why Parr didn’t nod toward other Red Sox legends. The answer, he said, was that some names were hard to get local approval for. Ted Williams, for example, had a surname common enough that there’s already a Camp Williams Road in town.
“Some of them are personal favorites,” Parr said of the player names. “I was a big fan of Nathan Eovaldi and his performance in 2018, so he’s on there. ... Boggs was the reason I started liking the Red Sox, so I had to get him. I was just trying to pick some names that meant something to me, and to the organization as well.”
It’s not the first time Parr has gotten creative with street names. Edge Homes takes on anywhere from 10 to 12 development projects a year, and naming all those streets can be “a little bit of a daunting task sometimes,” he said.
Aside from Red Sox players, Parr has also referenced comic book movie actors. A subdivision in Riverton, Utah, includes a Hemsworth Lane and a Hiddleston Drive, named after Chris Hemsworth and Tom Hiddleston, the actors who play Thor and Loki in Marvel films.
“My company encourages us to be creative,” he said. “It’s just something fun that we do as a team.”
Parr, who carries a Red Sox water bottle and owns a replica championship ring, has taken his family to a few games at Fenway. But he admits that Red Sox fans aren’t exactly plentiful in Salt Lake City.
“I’m kind of alone,” he said. “At the office, I would say there’s definitely more Yankees fans around me than Red Sox fans. But I’ll be a Red Sox fan till the day I die.”
At least one Herriman resident recognizes the significance of the street names.
Chris Watson, 56, a graphic designer and photographer, has lived in Utah for over two decades. But he was raised in Framingham, collecting Red Sox trading cards and watching Luis Tiant and Jim Rice and Carl Yastrzemski.
“I don’t keep up with [the team] as much anymore,” he said. “But the only baseball hat I’ll wear is a Red Sox hat.”
When he was searching for a place to build a new home a few years back, he realized “really quickly” the names on the lot were something special.
It was a “really fun coincidence” to end up living on Fisk Road — named after Carlton Fisk, Watson’s favorite player on the (in)famous 1978 team. Even that team, lamented for its end-of-season collapse against the Yankees, still holds a special place in his heart.
“That was the peak of fandom for my 8, 9-year old self,” he said. “He would have thought it was really cool [to be living here].”
Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.

item.content:encoded:
Not long after, the Braves beat the Astros, officially punching Boston’s ticket to the playoffs as one of the AL’s three Wild Card teams.
It’s a postseason appearance few saw coming when the Sox started the season 32-46. Not only are they the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 32 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it.
Currently sitting as the No. 5 seed, the Red Sox are most likely to open their playoff run with a best-of-three Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium, starting on Sept. 29. It would be a rematch from last year, when the Yankees won in three games after the Sox had taken the opener behind a brilliant performance by Garrett Crochet.
In a bit of baseball poetry, a home run swing from Mike Yastrzemski, the grandson of Red Sox legend Carl, gave the Braves a lead they would not relinquish and helped officially push Boston into the postseason.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, it was almost July [before we got going], and to fight as hard as we did, to put ourselves in the position we did, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” said interim manager Chad Tracy, who took over after the dismissal of Alex Cora on April 25. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
For several weeks, the Red Sox never stopped punching. The road back to contention started with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway from June 25-28.
It continued on July 3, when the Sox began what would become a winning streak of 15 games, tying the franchise record set by the 1946 pennant winners of Ted Williams, Bobby Doerr, Dom DiMaggio and Johnny Pesky.
And even after that streak was snapped, the Sox shortly thereafter ripped off another nine-game winning streak, giving them the best 30-game stretch in team history. Including the Yankees sweep that started it all, Boston was 32-5 from June 25-Aug. 7.
Just when the rabid fanbase known as Red Sox Nation thought they were losing their summer, Boston pulled off one of the most remarkable turnarounds in history, and got the first reward for that on Sunday.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
Roman Anthony couldn't put a ring on it. For more than two months, what had to have been one of the most annoying and nagging injuries kept Anthony out of the Boston Red Sox lineup. He had partially torn a ligament in his right ring finger. It wasn't some massive, noticeable, life-changing injury. It was just an ailment that made it really hard to swing a bat.
The Red Sox handled business in the meantime. They went on that franchise record-tying 15-game winning streak. They watched Ceddanne Rafaela become an All-Star. They saw Mickey Gasper temporarily turn into Ted Williams.
Then, in late August, Anthony came back. He was supposed to be the final piece to the puzzle. If the Red Sox were a good baseball team without Anthony, they could potentially be a great one with him -- at least, that's how the thinking went. The problem, though, is clear: Since Anthony has been back, he hasn't been quite right. He hasn't looked like a rising star. He's looked like a hitter who is recognizing that hitting is actually really, really hard.
There's not a whole lot of time for Anthony to right the ship before the postseason, but there's just enough time for Boston fans to hold out hope that he has (or will find) a solution.
If he's going to make fixes, it'll have to be in his approach at the plate, where he's whiffed at a 35% rate in September, including a stretch of 17 strikeouts in 35 plate appearances. Something clearly isn't quite right here, although it may not be as bad as you think.
Roman Anthony's Swing Looks Different When It Matters
One quick way to figure out what might be happening with a hitter who is striking out a lot is to fast forward directly to two-strike counts and see what's happening.
First, though, take a look at what Anthony looks like on the first pitch of an at-bat with two runners on base. This clip shows a wide stance that's slightly open, a strong leg kick, and Anthony's signature ability to stay through the baseball and drive it the other way:

Roman Anthony Since Returning From IL

AB: 61
R: 8
H: 16
HR: 3
RBI: 5
BB: 5
SO: 20
AVG: .262
OPS: .793 pic.twitter.com/zCDEPxL2xi

That's not the swing that Anthony has had lately on two strikes. If you want to be a sad Red Sox fan for a few minutes, this next video is for you (it shows Anthony's recent strikeout stretch). And if you watch closely, you'll see that not only is Anthony not setting up the same each time as on the hit in the video above. He's not even set up the same in all of these clips. Clearly, he's searching for a two-strike solution, but it's changing the openness of his stance, the height at which he stands, the level of his leg kick and even the apparent length of his swing:

Roman Anthony has struck out in 17 of his last 35 plate appearances, and his 2-strike approach has looked completely discombobulated. pic.twitter.com/r3q3tc5A64
— Stats (@redsoxstats) September 12, 2026
Some hitters change their approach with two strikes -- contact hitters in particular often get lower and choke up on the bat to have the best chance of putting the ball in play. But the big and strong Anthony, if he's going to do that, better at least stick to a plan. And it seems like right now he doesn't have one.
So we can see the video, and we can see the basic stats, but to further figure out what's been going wrong with Anthony, we decided to take a look at the metrics behind his swing itself.
Clearly, coming back from a finger injury and a long layoff could make hitting harder, but this isn't just about Anthony's .226 average and .677 OPS in September. The Red Sox need to figure out what's going on so they can address it and improve those numbers the rest of the way.
Lucky for us, Statcast has just about every metric you could possibly imagine, so it's possible to compare all sorts of things about Anthony's swing inputs and batted ball outputs from each month of his rookie season through right now.
Take, for example, his attack angle. That's the vertical direction the sweet spot is traveling when it hits the baseball. This month, Anthony has an attack angle of 16 degrees. When he had a .946 OPS in July of last year, it was 14 degrees. The only time it has ever been this high before was last September in a super small sample size (26 pitches seen). And while it may seem like a minor difference, it can prevent the ideal line drive from coming off Anthony's bat.
That's just one metric. The rest of his bat statistics actually seem fine. Nothing is weird about his bat speed or his swing length or his attack direction. There's nothing underlying there to be totally concerned about.
This is the part, Red Sox fans, where the news gets good.
Roman Anthony Is Actually Just Fine
Anthony's swing, while maybe a little tilted from its optimal self, doesn't seem broken. He's just whiffing a bit more than you'd want. It's also worth considering what happens when Anthony doesn't whiff.
When he's made contact the ball in September, Anthony has hit it harder than ever before. His previous best average exit velocity in a month was in July 2025, at 96.9 miles per hour.
Entering this week, Anthony has averaged 97.0 miles per hour of exit velocity on his batted balls in this month. He's had a hard-hit percentage of 63.6%, right about his career average, and he has the third-best single-month barrel rate of his career. The Red Sox obviously can't afford for him to keep whiffing on more than a third of the swings he takes, but we can also recognize that Anthony is oh so close to putting it back together again.
